title: A Book Read by the Rivers of Babylon
sum: The book opens with a story. In Babylon, in the fifth year after Jerusalem was burned, Baruch reads his book aloud to the exiled King Jeconiah and to all the exiles. They weep, fast and pray, collect money, and send it to Jerusalem with the silver vessels of the temple, asking the priests there to offer sacrifices, to pray for Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar, and to pray for the exiles. They send the book too, to be read out as a confession on feast days.

Then the confession begins (1:15). It follows the prayer of Daniel 9 phrase by phrase: righteousness belongs to God, shame belongs to us. From the Exodus until now, the people did not listen; so the curse that Moses wrote down has come true. The chapter's two halves fit together: a people who accept foreign rule as God's discipline (1:11–12) and a people who say plainly that the discipline is deserved (1:15–22).
readings: Read as history

Read as an account of real events, the chapter shows exiles in Babylon a few years after 586 BC keeping contact with the remnant in Jerusalem, sending money for worship at the ruined altar (as Jeremiah 41:5 shows others doing) and following Jeremiah's advice to pray for Babylon (Jeremiah 29:7). Those who read it this way explain the problems one by one: Baruch may have gone east later; Joakim may have been a leading priest, not the high priest; the vessels of Zedekiah may be a smaller return the other books do not record.
Read as a frame for a later prayer

Most critical scholars read 1:1–14 as a story written to introduce older prayers and poems, giving them the authority of Jeremiah's scribe. The frame has things that do not fit the 580s BC: Baruch in Babylon (Jeremiah 43:6 puts him in Egypt), a working altar in Jerusalem, Belshazzar as Nebuchadnezzar's son, as in Daniel 5. On this reading the frame tells later Jews how to live under a foreign empire: pray for its rulers, confess the nation's sins, support Jerusalem.

views.C: The Catholic Church holds Baruch as part of the Old Testament; the Council of Trent defined it as sacred and canonical, as Gigot's article for the Catholic Encyclopedia notes. Gigot defended Baruch's authorship while allowing that the book was compiled, as other biblical books were. The chapter's prayer for the rulers fits the Church's long practice of praying for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2).
views.O: In Orthodox Bibles Baruch follows Jeremiah, and the frame's picture of Jeremiah's scribe reading to the exiles is taken as part of the Jeremiah tradition. The confession that begins in 1:15 is a model of repentance for the whole people, not only for individuals.
views.P: Protestants, for whom the book is not Scripture, have usually pointed to the frame's historical problems (Baruch in Babylon, Belshazzar as Nebuchadnezzar's son) as one reason to read it as a later Jewish work. They value the confession as a witness to how Jews prayed after the exile.
views.H: Historical critics read 1:1–14 as a late frame. Toy noted the problems: the obscure "fifth year", Zedekiah's silver vessels, Belshazzar, and no reason to think Baruch was in Babylon; some writers in his day took Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar as stand-ins for the emperors Vespasian and Titus. He took "manna" in 1:10 as a sign that the first part was translated from Hebrew.
views.J: The book is not in the Jewish Bible, but its confession belongs to a kind of prayer that Jews prayed after the exile (Ezra 9, Nehemiah 9, Daniel 9), and that grew into the communal confessions of the synagogue. The Apostolic Constitutions claim that some Jews read Baruch with Lamentations in late summer; no Jewish source confirms it.

echoes: Jeremiah 29:7; Jeremiah 36:4–10; Jeremiah 43:6; 2 Kings 24:12–16; 2 Kings 25:8; Ezra 1:7; Ezra 6:10; Daniel 5:2; Daniel 9:4–11; Deuteronomy 28:15; 1 Timothy 2:1–2

settings.what: The frame: Baruch's book read to the exiles and sent to Jerusalem
settings.by: an unnamed narrator, writing of Baruch in the third person
settings.to: in the story, the exiles in Babylon by the river Sud, from King Jeconiah down, and through them the priests and people in Jerusalem
settings.when: "the fifth year" after the Chaldeans burned Jerusalem (about 581 BC on the book's own dating)
settings.why: To give the prayers and poems that follow the authority of Jeremiah's scribe, and to show the right response to exile: grief, fasting, prayer, gifts for Jerusalem, prayer for the foreign king, and public confession.
settings.readers: Who the first readers were depends on the date. Toy reports dates for the parts from the Maccabean period (100s BC) to after the Roman destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 (Kneucker and others). Gigot, defending the traditional view, took it as written in Babylon five years after the fall. Either way the readers were Jews living under foreign rule, many of them far from Judea, for whom Jerusalem's temple and its fall were the center of memory.
views: Written by Baruch in Babylon about 581 BC and sent to Jerusalem (Gigot, defending the traditional view).
A later frame written to introduce the confession and poems; Toy thought an editor of the Maccabean era combined the pieces, while Kneucker and others put parts after AD 70.

settings.to: Joakim the priest, the other priests and the people left in Jerusalem
settings.when: sent with the money and the temple vessels, on the tenth of Sivan
settings.why: To fund sacrifices at the altar, to ask for prayer for the Babylonian kings and for the exiles, and to have the enclosed confession read in the temple on feast days. It binds the scattered people and the homeland together in one act of worship.
settings.readers: For readers far from Judea, the message shows exiles and the homeland sharing one confession and one temple, and accepting foreign rule as God's will for a time.

settings.what: The confession of sins and prayer for mercy
settings.by: the people, in words the exiles send ("This is what you are to say")
settings.to: the Lord, read aloud in the temple before the assembled people
settings.when: "on the day of the feast and on the days of its season" (1:14)
settings.why: To say in public that the disaster is just, the covenant curse come true (1:20; 2:2), to plead for mercy on the ground of God's compassion alone (2:19, 2:27), and to claim the promise to Moses that the exiles would turn back and be brought home (2:29–35). Knowing that it was written for public worship explains its repetitions and its borrowing from Daniel 9 and Jeremiah: it is a liturgy built from Scripture.
settings.readers: Gigot saw in 1:14 a sign that the prayer was first composed in Hebrew for reading in the temple. Toy judged that it borrows from Daniel 9, which would put it after about 165 BC. Its readers were a people who had to explain to themselves why God's city had fallen.

title: Righteousness Belongs to the Lord
sum: The confession goes on. God carried out his word: no city ever suffered like Jerusalem, where, as Moses warned, people ate their own children. Israel became a disgrace among the nations, "underneath and not on top". Twice the prayer repeats its refrain: righteousness belongs to the Lord, shame to us (1:15; 2:6).

At 2:11 confession turns to petition. The people admit three kinds of sin and ask God to turn his fury away, for his own sake and for his name's sake, because the dead cannot praise him but the crushed and hungry can. They do not ask for mercy on the strength of their ancestors' good deeds. They recall how they refused Jeremiah's word to serve Babylon, and how the prophets' threats came true. Then they recall God's promise through Moses: in exile the people would come to their senses, and God would give them a heart and ears that listen, bring them back, and make an everlasting covenant with them.
readings: Read as covenant theology

The chapter reads the exile through Deuteronomy 28–30: disobedience brings the curses, and in exile repentance brings return. God is in the right throughout (2:9). The confession teaches that disaster is not the end of the covenant but part of it, with a promise at the far side.
Read as a liturgy made from Scripture

Almost every line comes from an older text: Daniel 9, Jeremiah 7, 8, 27, 32 and 36, Deuteronomy 28 and 30, Solomon's prayer in 1 Kings 8. The prayer is a mosaic, and its power for its first hearers lay in hearing God's own words given back to him.

views.C: Catholic readers find in the chapter the pattern of contrition: admitting sin without excuse, trusting only in God's mercy (2:19), and hoping for a new heart (2:31). The theme of God giving a heart that listens is read as grace going before human repentance.
views.O: Orthodox readers hear in the chapter the voice of repentance that fills the Church's services, and in 2:17–18, where the humble and broken give God glory, the spirit of the penitential psalms.
views.P: Protestant readers who know the book note how close its teaching on mercy stands to their own: the plea rests "on the strength of" nothing "our ancestors and our kings did right" (2:19) agrees with Daniel 9:18 and Titus 3:5. They read it as a witness to Jewish faith, not as Scripture.
views.H: Critics see the chapter as an anthology of Jeremiah and Deuteronomy, with the promise of 2:29–35 put in Moses' mouth. Toy reports that Kneucker and others read the ruined house of 2:26 as the second temple after AD 70, though Kneucker allowed an earlier date if part of 2:26 was added later.
views.J: Jewish readers will recognize the structure of the later confessions of the Day of Atonement and the fast days: we have sinned, we have done wrong; not for our merits but for your name. The book itself fell out of Jewish use, but the theology of the chapter is that of the synagogue.

echoes: Daniel 9:12–19; Deuteronomy 28:13; Deuteronomy 28:37; Deuteronomy 28:53; Deuteronomy 28:62; Deuteronomy 30:1–6; Leviticus 26:29; Lamentations 4:10; 1 Kings 8:47–50; Jeremiah 7:34; Jeremiah 8:1; Jeremiah 27:11–12; Jeremiah 32:36–41; Jeremiah 36:30; Psalm 6:5; Psalm 115:17

settings.what: The prophets' word quoted in the prayer: serve the king of Babylon
settings.by: the Lord, through his servants the prophets (in words close to Jeremiah 27 and 7:34)
settings.to: in the prophets' day, Zedekiah and the people of Judah before 586 BC; here repeated by the praying people
settings.when: recalled in the confession, after the disaster it warned of
settings.why: Quoting the warning the people refused makes the confession exact: they knew, and they did not listen (2:24). It also keeps Jeremiah's advice alive for exiles still living under a foreign king (1:11–12).
settings.readers: For readers under Persian, Greek or Roman rule, the quotation told them that accepting the foreign king's rule for a time could be obedience to God, not betrayal.

settings.what: The promise to Moses, quoted in the prayer
settings.by: the Lord, speaking through Moses (a free summary of Deuteronomy 28–30, Leviticus 26 and Jeremiah 32)
settings.to: in the story, the Israelites at the giving of the law; here claimed by the exiles
settings.when: recalled "on the day you commanded him to write your law"
settings.why: To ground the plea in God's own promise: exile was foreseen, and so were repentance, a new heart, return to the land and an everlasting covenant. The exiles ask God to do what he said.
settings.readers: For scattered Jews who had confessed the nation's sins, the promise said that their confession was the turning point God had foretold.

title: Where Wisdom Lives
sum: The prayer ends (3:1–8): "a soul hemmed in" cries to the Lord Almighty, who sits enthroned forever while his people perish; hear the prayer of the dead of Israel; remember your power, not our ancestors' wrongs.

Then the book changes voice. A poem in praise of wisdom begins with "Listen, Israel" (3:9). Why is Israel in a foreign land, as good as dead? Because it left the spring of wisdom. Where can wisdom be found? Not by rulers, merchants, the wise men of Teman, or the giants of old. No one climbed into the sky or crossed the sea to fetch her. Only the creator, who commands the light and the stars, knows her, and he gave her to Jacob his servant. "After this she was seen on earth and went about among human beings" (3:38), and 4:1 names her: the book of God's commands, the law that lasts forever.
readings: Read as a Jewish wisdom poem

The poem answers Job 28's question, where is wisdom?, with the answer of Sirach 24: wisdom is the law of Moses, given to Israel alone. Exile came because Israel left the law; return will come when Israel holds her again (4:1–2). On this reading 3:38 describes the law, God's wisdom, living among God's people.
Read as a prophecy of Christ

Many early Christians read 3:36–38 as a prophecy of the incarnation: the God beside whom no other is reckoned was seen on earth and lived among people. Cyprian quoted it under the heading "That Christ is God", and the Orthodox Church reads 3:36–4:4 at Vespers on Christmas Eve. On this reading the wisdom given to Israel points ahead to the Wisdom and Word of God who "became flesh" (John 1:14).

views.C: The Catholic lectionary reads 3:9–15 and 3:32–4:4 at the Easter Vigil, among the readings that tell the history of salvation before the gospel of the resurrection. The reading ends with 4:1–4, so the Church hears 3:38 together with the law and the wisdom given to Israel.
views.O: The Orthodox Church reads 3:36–4:4 at Vespers on the Eve of the Nativity, among the Old Testament readings that announce Christ's birth (the OCA lists it as "Jeremiah (Baruch 3:35-4:4)" in its own numbering). The service hears "This is our God ... After this he was seen on earth" of the Son born in Bethlehem.
views.P: Protestants, for whom Baruch is not Scripture, read the poem as an important witness to the Jewish idea of wisdom as Torah that lies behind John 1 and Paul's calling Christ the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). They do not use 3:38 as proof of the incarnation.
views.H: Critics read the poem as a separate work from the prose before it, a wisdom hymn drawing on Job 28, Proverbs 8 and Deuteronomy 30, of the same kind as Sirach 24. Toy took 3:38 as a Christian addition. Others keep it as original and read it of wisdom as the law.
views.J: The poem's claim that wisdom is the Torah and lives in Israel is the claim of later Jewish teaching, for which the Torah was the wisdom by which God made the world (Genesis Rabbah 1:1). Read this way the poem ends in pure joy: "How happy we are, Israel!" (4:4).

deep.b:
The question has three answers, and each has a long history.

Wisdom given as the law. The grammar points this way. The "way of understanding" that God gave Jacob in 3:37 is feminine in Greek ("he gave her"), and the next words are "She is the book of the commands of God" (4:1). The verse would then say that wisdom, once hidden, became visible on earth and lived among people in the form of the law given to Israel. Proverbs has Wisdom say "my delights were with human beings" (Proverbs 8:31), and Sirach has her told to pitch her tent in Jacob (Sirach 24:8). This is the reading the Plain follows.

God seen on earth. The Greek verb has no subject word, and "he was seen" is also possible. The Latin reads visus est ("he was seen") and the KJV "Afterward did he shew himself upon earth". Many early Christians took the subject to be "our God" of 3:36 and read the verse of the Son. Cyprian quoted 3:36–38 in his Testimonies under the heading "That Christ is God"; the Apostolic Constitutions (5.20) quoted it as a prophecy of Christ; Hippolytus argued against Noetus, who used the passage to say that the Father himself had appeared on earth, that it speaks of the Son. The Orthodox Church reads the passage at Christmas.

A Christian addition. Crawford Toy, in the Jewish Encyclopedia, called the verse "undoubtedly a Christian interpolation". No Greek manuscript in Swete's notes lacks it, so the claim rests on its content and on how well it fits the Christian reading, not on manuscripts.

No church teaching document read for this page addresses the question directly, and the churches that hold Baruch as Scripture both read the passage in worship, the Orthodox at Christmas and the Catholics at Easter. So there is no "Where Christians differ" card here: the difference is between ways of reading, not between churches' teachings.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Baruch walks through Deuteronomy 30
deep.b: Deuteronomy 30 has three movements: in exile the people take God's words to heart and turn back (Deuteronomy 30:1–2); God gathers them from the nations and brings them home (Deuteronomy 30:3–5); and the commandment is not far off, not in the sky or across the sea, but near (Deuteronomy 30:11–14), so they must choose life (Deuteronomy 30:15–19). Baruch's three parts may follow the same order of ideas, though not of verses: the confession, ending with the promise that in exile "they will come to their senses" (2:30, Deuteronomy 30:1); the wisdom poem, with its sky and sea (3:29–30, Deuteronomy 30:12–13) and its "commandments of life" (3:9; 4:1, Deuteronomy 30:15); and the consolation, with the children gathered from east and west (4:37; 5:5, Deuteronomy 30:3–4). If so, the editor who joined the pieces read them as one sermon on Deuteronomy 30 for exiles. The links to Deuteronomy 30 in each part are well known; whether the order of the whole book was meant to follow that chapter is my own suggestion, and I have not found it argued in the sources read for this page.

echoes: Lamentations 5:19–20; Deuteronomy 6:4; Deuteronomy 30:11–19; Job 28; Job 38:7; Job 38:35; Proverbs 8:22–31; Jeremiah 2:13; Jeremiah 49:7; Genesis 6:4; Isaiah 40:26; Psalm 147:19–20; Sirach 24; John 1:14; John 3:13; Romans 10:6–8

settings.what: The last part of the prayer: "Lord Almighty, hear"
settings.by: the people in exile, praying as one
settings.to: the Lord Almighty, God of Israel
settings.why: To end the confession with the people's own state: hemmed in, worn out, as good as dead, still praising God and asking him to remember his power and name rather than their ancestors' sins. The repeated "in our exile" ties the prayer to the frame.
settings.readers: For a people living after the exile and far from Judea, it gave words for feeling forgotten while still holding on to God.

settings.by: an unnamed teacher of Israel, speaking in the manner of the wisdom books
settings.to: "Israel", the people in a foreign land
settings.when: in exile (3:10), with no named occasion
settings.why: To explain the exile as the result of leaving wisdom, and to call Israel back to her: the wisdom no nation found is the law Israel already holds (4:1). Knowing the hearers were exiles changes the tone: the poem is not a lecture to the comfortable but a reason for hope to people who thought themselves as good as dead.
settings.readers: Critical scholars treat the poem as a separate composition, perhaps from the 100s BC (Toy thought the early Maccabean period fits), joined to the confession by an editor; Kneucker and others put it after AD 70. Its readers were Jews tempted by the wisdom of other peoples, who needed to hear that the Torah was their wisdom.
views: A poem from the 100s BC or before, against the attraction of Greek learning (Toy).
Kneucker and other scholars of Toy's day dated it after the Roman capture of Jerusalem.

title: A Mother's Farewell and Her Hope
sum: After the poem, a new voice comforts the people: "Take heart, my people" (4:5). You were sold to the nations not to be destroyed but because you angered God by sacrificing to demons; you forgot God who fed you and grieved Jerusalem who nursed you.

Then Jerusalem herself speaks (4:9–29), a widowed mother. To the towns around her she mourns the captivity of her sons and daughters; to her children she says goodbye, "Walk on, children", and promises that the Everlasting who brought the disaster will rescue them soon. From 4:30 the poet turns to her: "Take heart, Jerusalem". The cities that enslaved her children will be miserable, burned and left to demons; and her sons are already coming home from the east.
readings: Read as a poem of consolation

Jerusalem the mother and the comfort of Isaiah 40–66 shape the chapter: the city is a widow, her children are taken, but God is her Savior and will give them back with joy. It answers Lamentations, where no one comforts her (Lamentations 1:2), with the comfort Isaiah promised (Isaiah 40:1).
Read for later readers

Babylon is never named in 4:30–35. For readers living centuries after the exile, the "miserable city" could be any empire that had scattered Jerusalem's children, and some scholars read it as Rome. The promise is that every such empire will be judged and emptied.

views.C: Catholic readers, who hold the chapter as Scripture, can hear mother Jerusalem with Paul's "The Jerusalem above ... is our mother" (Galatians 4:26), and her patient hope as a model for prayer in times of loss.
views.O: Orthodox readers hear in the mother city the voice of the Church grieving and hoping for her children, and in the return from the east the light that rises in Christ.
views.P: Protestant readers see the chapter as a Jewish reworking of Isaiah's comfort and of Lamentations, with its theology of discipline and return; they read it alongside its sources rather than as Scripture.
views.H: Critics read 4:5–5:9 as a third composition, built from Isaiah 40–66, Lamentations and Deuteronomy 32, perhaps by a different hand from the wisdom poem. Its date is tied to the question of its link with Psalms of Solomon 11 (see 5:5).
views.J: The picture of mother Zion weeping for her children and comforted by God runs through Jewish tradition, from Lamentations and Isaiah 54 to the later readings of comfort after the Ninth of Av, which come from Isaiah 40–66.

echoes: Deuteronomy 32:17–18; Deuteronomy 32:30; Deuteronomy 28:49–50; Lamentations 1:1–2; Lamentations 1:16; Isaiah 13:21–22; Isaiah 34:14; Isaiah 43:5–6; Isaiah 47:8–9; Isaiah 49:18–21; Isaiah 50:1; Isaiah 54:1–8; Isaiah 60:4; Isaiah 62:2; Jeremiah 50:39; 1 Corinthians 10:20; Galatians 4:26; Revelation 18:2

settings.what: The poet's word of comfort to the people
settings.by: an unnamed poet speaking for God ("my people")
settings.to: the exiles, "you who keep Israel's name alive"
settings.when: in exile, after the confession and the wisdom poem
settings.why: To turn the people from shame to courage: the exile is discipline, not destruction, and the cause is known (4:6–8).
settings.readers: For scattered Jews, it said that their scattering had a cause and an end.

settings.what: Jerusalem's lament and farewell to her children
settings.by: Jerusalem, pictured as a widowed mother
settings.to: first the towns around Zion (4:9–16), then her children going into exile (4:17–29)
settings.when: as the captives are led away (4:19)
settings.why: To make the loss felt as a mother's loss, and to give her children a mother's charge: be patient, cry out to God, turn back to him ten times over, and wait for his salvation "soon". The children who hear it are the exiles, so her farewell is also her promise to them.
settings.readers: Later readers, many living far from Judea, heard their mother city speak to them directly, as one who still waited for them.

settings.what: Comfort for Jerusalem: her enemies judged and her children brought home
settings.by: the poet, with God speaking in 4:34 ("I will take away")
settings.why: To answer her lament: the city that took her children will be emptied, and her children are coming from the east in glory. The poem dresses her for their arrival.
settings.readers: For readers under later empires the promise was open-ended: every power that scattered Jerusalem's children would fall, and God would gather them. Toy left open whether the close of the poem borrowed from Psalms of Solomon 11 (about 48 BC) or the other way round.

title: Jerusalem, Dressed for Her Children
sum: The book of Baruch proper ends in joy. Jerusalem is told to take off her mourning and put on the beauty of God's glory, his righteousness as a cloak and his glory as a turban. God will show her splendor to the whole world and give her a new name, "Peace of Righteousness" and "Glory of Godliness".

She is to stand on the heights and look east: her children are coming, gathered from west to east. They left on foot as prisoners; God brings them back carried in glory like a royal throne. The mountains are made low and the valleys filled for them, as in Isaiah 40, and the forests give them shade. God leads Israel home by the light of his glory, with his mercy and his righteousness. The righteousness that the confession gave to God alone (1:15) is now his gift to his people.
readings: Read as the return from Babylon

The chapter retells Isaiah's promises of a road through the desert and a joyful return, and for readers after 538 BC part of it had happened. It gave them a picture of the return still unfinished: a scattered people gathered and a glorious Jerusalem.
Read as the hope of the last days

Christian readers have read the chapter with Revelation 21, the new Jerusalem dressed as a bride, and with the gathering of the nations to Christ. Luke's use of the leveling of the mountains for John the Baptist (Luke 3:5) gave Christians a way to hear 5:7 as the preparation of the way of the Lord.

views.C: Catholic readers, who hold the chapter as Scripture, hear its leveled road with John the Baptist's call to prepare the way of the Lord, since Luke uses the same words of Isaiah 40 for him (Luke 3:4–6).
views.O: Orthodox readers hear Jerusalem's new clothing and name as the glory of the Church and of the soul made new in Christ, a theme of the services of feasts.
views.P: Protestant readers compare the chapter with Isaiah 40, 49, 52, 60 and 62, which it reworks, and read it as an early Jewish witness to the hope of the gathering of Israel.
views.H: The close parallels with Psalms of Solomon 11 are the chief clue for dating the end of the book. Toy left open which was the borrower. Both build on Isaiah 40 and 60.
views.J: The return of the exiles, the leveled road and the gathered children remained a central Jewish hope, prayed for daily in the later synagogue prayer for the ingathering of the exiles.

echoes: Isaiah 40:3–5; Isaiah 49:22; Isaiah 52:1–2; Isaiah 52:12; Isaiah 55:12; Isaiah 60:1–4; Isaiah 61:10; Isaiah 62:2–3; Jeremiah 33:16; Psalms of Solomon 11:1–9; Luke 3:4–6; Revelation 21:2
